Immutability is the claim that God never changes in any way. The strain is that the things the tradition also says God does (beginning to create, answering a prayer, becoming incarnate) are all transitions from one state to another. Keeping the action-language while denying God any transition leaves the verbs owing an account of how their direction and contingency arise from an unchanging source.

*What the tradition holds.* Classical theology holds that God is immutable: God does not change, cannot change, and does not undergo any sort of intrinsic variation across time, situation, or relation (Aquinas, *ST* I.9.1; Augustine, *Confessions* XI; Anselm, *Proslogion* XXII). The doctrine has Aristotelian roots in the unmoved mover (*Metaphysics* Λ.7) and binds tightly to simplicity (§6.2.1), necessity (§6.3.1), and pure actuality: a simple, necessary, fully actual being has no potency to be otherwise, and so does not change. Contemporary defenders include Dolezal [-@dolezal2017], Feser [-@feser2017], Weinandy [-@weinandy2000], and Stump [-@stump2003]; the doctrine has been refined into *weak immutability* [@mullins2016; @pawl2020] that distinguishes intrinsic from relational change. The position immutability has traditionally held, fully stated, is that God's intrinsic state (essence, knowledge, will, relations to creatures) is invariant across any possible difference in creaturely state, and that the apparent changes in God's relations to creatures (becoming the creator of *this* world rather than another, becoming incarnate, responding to prayer) are *Cambridge changes* (mere shifts in how God stands related to a changing world, involving no alteration in God) rather than real changes in God.

*What cannot be answered.* Five questions confront immutability with what the doctrine, in the form structural reasoning reaches, cannot answer. What underlies the five is structural: the difference between *acting* and *being acted upon* depends on directed transition, and the doctrine's strategy is to deny directed transition of the divine being while preserving the action-language the believer's life rests on.

**Q1.** *How does a being that cannot change begin to create?* Pure actuality (the property of having no unrealized potential) is the metaphysical floor of immutability (Aquinas, *ST* I.3.1). Creation requires a transition in the creature from not existing to existing. Whether it also requires intrinsic transition in the cause is precisely what the classical timeless-causation model denies. The classical reply locates the transition entirely in the creature: God eternally wills the creature; the creature comes to be in time; God does not undergo any change in the willing (Aquinas, *ST* I.46.1; *SCG* II.35). The concern here is that the eternal willing of a temporal creation is the relational structure the believer's prayer life and providence rest on: prayer at t_1 that affects God's relation to the world at t_2. The Cambridge-change reply preserves God's intrinsic invariance by relocating the variance into the creature, but religious language of deliberation and response can suggest intrinsic change. The issue is whether that language is literal, analogical, or accommodated to creaturely perspective; intuition alone does not settle it.

**Q2.** *How does a mind that never changes know that the present has changed?* If God knows that *Caesar crosses the Rubicon* before, during, and after the crossing, the *knowledge-content* differs by tense even if the *fact* is timeless. The classical reply is that God knows the timeless fact and that the tensed truths are creaturely modes of access to the same fact (Aquinas, *ST* I.14.13; [@stumpKretzmann1981; @helm2010]). The concern here is that a being who knows *that Caesar crosses the Rubicon* without knowing *that Caesar will cross* or *has crossed* either lacks information the creature has (in which case omniscience fails) or has the tensed information by some mode the timeless-fact reading does not deliver [@prior1959; @kretzmann1966; @mullins2016]. The Boethian reply (eternal vision of all times at once) preserves immutability by relocating God outside time, which makes the tense-bearing structure of knowing about a temporal world the structural feature the doctrine forecloses.

**Q3.** *How does the maker undergo no transition, when making is the transition?* The creature comes from non-being to being. The classical reply treats the transition as entirely in the creature: it is the creature that transitions; God neither pre-exists the act in any tensed sense (atemporality) nor changes by performing it (immutability). The concern here is that *bringing-into-being* is the paradigm of directed transition (§2.6.2): the act has a *from* (nothing) and a *to* (the creature), and the directedness is what the act consists in. To attribute the act to an unchanged agent requires an account of how causal direction and contingent effect arise from one invariant intention. It is not semantically empty merely because the transition occurs in the effect. The reply that God is the *terminus a quo* (the starting point *from which*) of the transition without undergoing it makes the *acting* into a structural feature of the world's hosting of the act, not of the agent's performing it.

**Q4.** *How does the unchangeable become flesh?* The doctrine of the incarnation holds that the second person of the Trinity *became* man (*ho logos sarx egeneto*, John 1:14). The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined the union as one person in two natures, fully divine and fully human. The classical reply is that the incarnation is a change in the human nature, not in the divine nature: the divine Word does not become human in the sense of acquiring a property, but human nature becomes the Word's nature in the sense of being assumed (Aquinas, *ST* III.16; Cyril of Alexandria, *On the Unity of Christ*). The concern here is that *assumption* is itself a directed transition: there is a *before* the assumption (in which the human nature does not exist as the Word's) and an *after* (in which it does). The reply that the assumption is eternal in the divine register and temporal in the human register locates the directedness in the human register only, which makes the *becoming* of John 1:14 a structural feature of the human side; the divine side is what *does not become* anything.

**Q5.** *How is a change in God's relations not a change in God?* Pawl [-@pawl2020] and Mullins [-@mullins2016] develop *weak immutability*: God does not change in essential properties or intrinsic state, but does change in accidental or relational properties (e.g., becoming-the-creator-of-this-world, being-prayed-to, becoming-incarnate). The concern here is that *change in relational properties* is what *real change in relations* names, and the classical doctrine's whole strategy has been to deny real relations between God and creatures (Aquinas, *ST* I.13.7; *SCG* II.12). The weak-immutability refinement admits variance back into the divine being's relations, which is what the strong doctrine refused. The refinement is honest about what the believer's intuition requires; the concern here is that what the refinement admits is the directed transition the strong doctrine was preserving against. The temporalist repair pressed from inside the literature (drop strong immutability but keep a temporal, personal God, rather than continue to the dipolar terminus) is the live alternative engaged at §6.7.3 (with the temporality structure at §6.3.2); the concern this section presses is that weak immutability's *internal* logic, once relational variance is admitted, runs on to the dipolar assignment Q5 turns to next. Hartshorne's dipolar theism occupies the logical terminus of the weak-immutability move and gives it a principled stopping point: the abstract pole is strictly immutable in the classical sense (no intrinsic change, no relational change, no variance of any kind) while the concrete pole is genuinely responsive, growing with the world's cumulative creative advance and bearing the directed transitions the believer's life rests on (*The Divine Relativity* [-@hartshorne1948]; *Omnipotence and Other Theological Mistakes* [-@hartshorne1984]). The dipolar account does not blur strong and weak immutability; it assigns each cleanly to a different pole of a single subject. The concern here is the one §5.3.3 presses: the relation between the poles is a directed, asymmetric crossing, and the abstract pole enters a determinate relation with the concrete pole. That creates a differentiation and dependence burden, though a relation need not be a transition undergone by both relata. The crossing obtains only within T, S, and Φ, as §5.3.3 shows; the dipolar assignment relocates the immutability problem into the pole-relation rather than resolving it.

*What is required.* Taken together, the five pressures expose what *immutable* requires. Pure actuality relocates the transition into the creature and construes divine agency through invariant causation. The burden is to explain contingent effects and real causal asymmetry without intrinsic divine change. Tensed knowledge of contingents requires either the tense-bearing structure the doctrine forecloses or a Boethian timeless vision that makes the believer's intuition of God-as-responding to temporal events a feature of the creature's access, not the divine knowing. Creatio ex nihilo is a directed transition in the effect; an immutable-agent account must explain how its source grounds that directedness without undergoing it. The Chalcedonian incarnation requires a *becoming* that the strong doctrine relocates into the human nature, leaving the divine register as the bearer of an action it does not perform. Weak immutability admits relational variance, which is the variance the strong doctrine was preserving against. The five pressures leave a distinction between invariance of character or essence, strict absence of intrinsic change, and invariance of structural conditions. These should not be collapsed into one predicate.

*What is inverted.* Immutability is the structural status of the modal structure. *Does not change*, in the only sense that survives the dilemmas above, names not the invariance of a being but the necessity of a structure: the modal structure □(T∧S∧Φ) is what it is in every possible world because what *possible world* means is *consistent with the structure*. The structure's invariance is not an absence of motion in a being lacking all potency; it is the necessity of the conditions of any motion at all. Immutability's facet of that necessity is specifically temporal: not that the structure holds across every world, but that within any world there is no moment at which T, S, and Φ alter, because succession is something they condition rather than undergo. The action-language the believer's life rests on (creation, providence, response to prayer, incarnation) lives at the level of T, S, Φ: directed transitions of substances within the necessary structure. Those transitions occur within Nature. Calling Nature itself their agent would require an additional theory of agency and should not be inferred from structural hosting alone. The type/token distinction (§7.7) keeps this exact: it is type-necessary that the structure produce operations of this kind (that there be transitions, agents, and the loop that takes up what Nature contains) while which particular operations occur is token-contingent. *Immutable* names the frame's invariance; that necessity reaches the kind of working the structure must host, not the particular tokens, and the believer's action-language lives among the tokens. Pressed for what makes it coherent, *immutable* names the modal-structure necessity that is the condition of any change at all: not the stillness of a being, but the necessity of the structure within which motion happens.
